scoring.subdimension_score: Each question measures one subdimension. The chosen option is the subdimension score, a whole number from 0 to 5.
scoring.dont_know: 'I do not know' gives a score of 0 and sets the flag 'insufficient_evidence', as in the chatbot.
scoring.aggregation: Dimension and overall scores, rounding and the report follow the same rules as the chatbot (Sections 2.4 and 2.5).

items.question: How do employees in your organization typically find the data they need?

options.text: Data is very hard or impossible to find. There is no way to locate it, formal or informal, and nobody has seen this as a problem.
Finding data takes a lot of effort, such as many inquiries or searching scattered sources, and whether it works depends on who is searching.
Data is usually found through informal channels, such as asking a colleague who knows it or lists kept by a team, but this depends on specific people.
There is a documented, organization-wide way to find data, such as a data catalog or central inventory, with standard procedures and contact points.
There is an organization-wide data catalog or inventory, and someone responsible checks regularly that it is complete and up to date.
Search results and feedback from employees are used to make the data catalog easier to use, and new datasets are added to it automatically when they are created.
I do not know

items.question: How is responsibility for data handled in your organization?

options.text: There is no concept of data ownership. Nobody is responsible for any data, formally or informally, and this has not been seen as a problem.
No one clearly owns the data. Many people use it, and someone takes responsibility only when a problem occurs, so whether data is maintained varies.
Within teams, people generally know who looks after which data, usually whoever created or uses it, but this is not written down and differs between teams.
Every key dataset has an owner, formally assigned and documented according to one standard for the whole organization and tied to roles rather than people.
Owners are formally assigned and documented, and ownership is reviewed regularly, so datasets without an owner or owners who have left are found and fixed.
Assigning an owner is built into how data is created, so every new dataset has an owner from the start, and the rules change when reviews show problems.
I do not know

items.question: How is data quality handled in your organization, and how usable is the data for analysis or AI?

options.text: Data quality is not managed and has not been seen as a problem. Data is so inconsistent that it cannot be used without being rebuilt.
There are no quality rules. Individuals fix problems when they notice them, usually for one task, and data needs extensive manual cleaning before every use.
Some teams have informal rules and repeat basic checks on their own data, but quality differs between teams, and combining data from different systems needs significant cleaning.
Documented quality rules apply across the whole organization, with assigned responsibilities, so data from different systems is consistent and can be used with limited preparation.
Organization-wide quality rules are enforced through system controls such as required fields, quality is measured against defined targets, and problems are found and corrected.
Recurring quality problems are fixed at their source instead of being cleaned up each time, and most checks run automatically. Data can be used for analysis or AI without extra preparation.
I do not know

items.question: How do people in your organization approach AI, in their attitude and in their daily work?

options.text: AI is not used or discussed. Employees have no access to AI tools, and openness to AI has not been seen as something that needs attention.
A few individuals try AI tools on their own, often free versions, without permission or guidance; most employees lack the knowledge or confidence to use AI.
Some teams or departments use AI regularly for specific purposes and encourage experimenting, while others remain skeptical or uninvolved, depending on individual managers.
AI is part of regular work across departments, with approved tools and shared guidelines, and employees are invited to propose and test ideas for using AI.
AI is used across the organization, and its adoption and employees' attitudes are tracked, for example through usage data or surveys, so that low adoption is addressed.
Trying out AI is a normal part of everyday work. Employees regularly propose and test new ideas and share with others what worked and what did not.
I do not know

items.question: Who in your organization has the skills to develop or implement AI?

options.text: No one inside or outside the organization, and the need has not been recognized.
Only a few self-taught individuals; AI is not part of anyone's role.
Some teams have AI specialists or work with external experts, mostly without involving business experts.
AI roles are defined across the organization, and AI work combines technical, business and subject-matter expertise.
AI skills and capacity are assessed regularly, and gaps are closed through hiring, training or partners.
There are career paths for AI roles, and the way the organization hires, develops and keeps AI experts is adapted based on what works.
I do not know

items.question: How do employees in your organization learn to work with AI?

options.text: There is no AI training or support. Nobody has considered that employees might need it, so no one plans or offers any learning about AI.
Employees learn about AI on their own, for example from online videos or by trying tools. There is no training, guidance or sharing of experience.
Some teams have occasional learning, for example a workshop or a colleague showing how they use ChatGPT. It is not organized for the whole organization.
All employees have a structured AI training program, such as online courses for their role, and practical guides for the approved tools. Someone is responsible for it.
There is a structured AI training program, and its outcomes are measured. For example, participation and skills before and after training are tracked, and gaps are fixed.
Learning about AI is part of daily work, for example through an AI community or regular sharing sessions, and courses are updated whenever new AI tools appear.
I do not know

items.question: Has your organization defined what it wants to achieve with AI?

options.text: No, and leadership is not interested in defining it.
No; individuals have ideas, but nothing is defined.
Some leaders or departments have their own goals for AI, but there is no shared ambition.
A documented AI ambition or strategy for the whole organization states the role AI should play and is communicated to everyone.
The ambition is reviewed regularly, at least once a year, against progress and changes such as new regulation.
The AI ambition actively shapes the organization's long-term direction and is updated whenever results or new developments in AI call for it.
I do not know

items.question: How is AI connected to your organization's business goals?

options.text: It is not; AI is not considered, or only as a technical topic.
AI is a technical experiment; any objectives are vague, such as "become AI-driven".
Some leaders connect AI to goals in their own area, but without measurable targets.
AI objectives are measurable business targets linked to the strategy, with an executive sponsor and a budget.
Leadership reviews progress against the targets regularly, and missed targets are addressed.
AI objectives are part of every strategic planning cycle, and new targets are set based on what earlier AI projects achieved.
I do not know

items.question: How does your organization decide which AI ideas to pursue?

options.text: It does not; no one has considered where AI could bring value.
Ideas start ad hoc from individual interest or available tools, without any assessment.
Teams choose and fund their own AI projects, each judging them in their own way.
An organization-wide process assesses ideas against criteria such as business value and feasibility, and a designated body decides.
The results of AI projects are measured against their expected value, and weak projects are adjusted or stopped.
Lessons from past AI projects are used to sharpen how ideas are selected, and the organization actively looks for new places where AI could help.
I do not know

items.question: How well do your organization's systems support the use of AI?

options.text: Systems are outdated or isolated and cannot support AI, and this has not been considered.
There are only basic services provided by the organization; AI is used only through public tools, and data is moved by hand.
Some teams have the systems and tools they need for AI, but systems differ and are mostly not connected.
A common technical environment for the whole organization provides approved AI services, and key systems are connected.
The environment is monitored for availability, performance, usage and costs, and problems are resolved.
AI solutions can be deployed and scaled automatically, and the environment is adapted as new AI needs appear.
I do not know

items.question: How does your organization obtain AI tools and solutions?

options.text: It has not obtained any and has not considered how it would.
Individuals choose tools themselves, often free versions, without approval.
Teams buy or build their own solutions, without coordination.
A common approach evaluates tools and vendors against defined criteria, and approved tools and contracts are managed centrally.
Vendors, costs and licence use are monitored, and problems are addressed.
Experience with vendors and tools is used to update the selection criteria, and decisions to build or buy are reviewed as needs change.
I do not know

items.question: How does your organization protect its data when employees use AI tools?

options.text: There are no rules for protecting data when AI is used. Anyone can enter confidential or personal data into any AI tool, and nobody sees this as a risk.
A few people protect sensitive data on their own, for example by not pasting customer data into AI tools. There are no rules, and access to data is not controlled.
Some teams have their own rules, for example a list of allowed AI tools or limits on who can see certain data. Other teams have none, and nobody checks the rules.
An organization-wide policy defines which data may be used in which AI tools. Data is classified, for example as public, internal or confidential, and people get access only to what they need.
Access to data and the use of AI tools are reviewed regularly, for example who accessed which data and whether AI use meets legal requirements such as GDPR. Problems are fixed.
Lessons from reviews, incidents and new regulations are used to update the security rules. Monitoring is largely automated, for example alerts when sensitive data is sent to an AI tool.
I do not know
